newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vol curves flatten as dlr weakens.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vol curves flatten as dlr weakens.

text.p: The inverted dollar/mark volatility curve and the positively sloped dollar/yen curve both flattened after the greenback tested lows early before clawing back up slightly in U.S. trading, dealers said.

While most traders still believed the big risk was still to the dollar's upside, at least in dollar/mark, they noted growing concern that the U.S. currency could be due for a significant pullback after the strong gains this year.
"The curves are flatter and vols are a little bit softer, but it really depends on whether or not these support levels in the dollar hold," said a European bank trader in Chicago.
"I think most people are waiting to see what comes out of Humphrey-Hawkins (testimony by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan on Wednesday and Thursday)," he added.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark was about 0.1 point below late Friday levels at 9.7/9.9 percent in early afternoon U.S. business. One-year was little changed at 9.45/9.65 percent.

A gradually dwindling actual day-to-day volatility was making it tough to hold on to shorter-dated options, which have higher gamma and are sensitive to spot rate gyrations but also vulnerable to time decay, traders said.
"People still don't want to be short options, but they probably don't need a whole lot of gamma right now," said a U.S. bank trader.
In dollar/yen, on the other hand, one-month volatility was unchanged from Friday at 10.7/10.9 percent, while one-year edged down slightly to 10.9/11.2 percent.

Fears of a steeper slide in spot underpinned the front end, traders said. The dollar fell to about 121.60 yen earlier, the lowest level since February 10, when it tumbled on news the Group of Seven industrial nations declared that the dollar's correction from its 1995 lows was over.

Concerns over dollar-asset repatriation by Japanese corporations ahead of their March 31 fiscal year-end was fuelled by news that Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Ltd would liquidate all its dollar-denominated deposits, currently standing at about $700 million, and convert them into yen.
Risk reversals, which reflect pricing differential between puts and calls, shifted clearly in favor of yen puts in dollar/yen, with one-month 25-delta at 0.1/0.4 percent skewed for yen calls.
One-month 25-delta dollar/mark risk reversal was at around par, after having favored mark puts for most of the year.
